claim.pdf_says: 15.68.4   Returned value rules  — printed in the same subclause style as 15.68.1 General / 15.68.2 General format / 15.68.3 Argument rules (all fourth-level subclauses of 15.68 NUMVAL-C function)
claim.markdown_says: ## 15.68.4 Returned value rules   (line 37121 of specs/ISO_COBOL.md — H2), whereas '### 15.68.1 General' (37021), '### 15.68.2 General format' (37028) and '### 15.68.3 Argument rules' (37036) are H3
claim.why_it_matters: Same as 15.67.4: the H2 promotes a subclause to clause level, breaking the 15.68 outline and making the NUMVAL-C returned-value rules look like a separate top-level clause.

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED on both sides, with one correction to how it was labelled.

PDF side (rendered p927 @300dpi, printed folio 897): the heading reads '15.68.4   Returned value rules' in bold, at body-text size, with the number/tab/title spacing used for three-component subclause headings. Rendering p925 (folio 895) for comparison shows '15.68 NUMVAL-C function', then '15.68.1   General', '15.68.2   General format' and '15.68.3   Argument rules' in that identical bold style. The clause heading 15.68 and its subclauses are typographically near-identical in this document, so the PDF's own evidence for the level is the section NUMBER (three components = fourth-level subclause), not the typeface. 15.68.4 is unambiguously a sibling of 15.68.1-.3 and a child of 15.68.

Markdown side (verified by direct read of specs/ISO_COBOL.md): line 37121 is '## 15.68.4 Returned value rules' (H2); lines 37021, 37028 and 37036 are '### 15.68.1 General', '### 15.68.2 General format' and '### 15.68.3 Argument rules' (H3); the parent at line 37018 is '## 15.68 NUMVAL-C function' (H2). Every line number and quotation in the claim is exact. Only one 15.68.4 heading exists in the file, so this is not a duplicate-anchor artifact.

Not refutable on the usual grounds: no text is lost or reflowed, but the defect alleged is a level error, not lost text; it is not a page-break, wrap or hyphenation artifact; and it cannot be defended as a deliberate flattening convention because the three immediate siblings ten lines earlier in the same clause use H3. Repo-wide the convention is decisive: 364 three-component '15.x.y' headings are H3 against 12 at H2, and 15.68.4 is one of the 12 outliers (the others include the directly analogous 15.67.4 and 15.69.4).

Why this is structural rather than cosmetic: in a Markdown transcription the heading depth is the only encoding of clause hierarchy. An H2 here makes 15.68.4 a sibling of clause 15.68 instead of its child, so any derived table of contents, outline, or 'extract everything under 15.68' range query drops the returned-value rules from the NUMVAL-C clause. Scoping honestly: it corrupts the document tree only — the normative COBOL semantics of the NUMVAL-C returned value are unaffected, and the rule text on this page (1) through 3)) transcribes faithfully.
verdict.corrected_description: Real, but the kind label 'missing-heading' is wrong and should be 'heading-level' (or 'wrong-heading-depth'). Nothing is missing: the heading '15.68.4 Returned value rules' is present at line 37121 with its number and title transcribed verbatim. The defect is its depth — it is emitted as H2 ('## 15.68.4 Returned value rules') while its three siblings in the same clause are H3 (15.68.1 at 37021, 15.68.2 at 37028, 15.68.3 at 37036) and its parent 15.68 is itself H2 at 37018. The fix is a one-character change, '##' -> '###', at line 37121. Note the PDF prints clause and subclause headings in effectively the same bold body-size style, so the level is established by the three-component section number rather than by typography — the claim's 'printed in the same subclause style as 15.68.1' overstates what the glyphs alone prove, though the conclusion it draws is correct. This is one instance of a small pattern: 15.67.4 (line 37005) and 15.69.4 (line 37189) carry the identical H2 defect, and all three should be swept in one change set; 15.69.4 additionally reads 'Returned values rules', which needs separate checking against its own page. Impact is confined to the derived outline/TOC and section-range extraction; no normative NUMVAL-C text is altered.
